claims.summary: For inflammation, Collagen has moderate human evidence (33 studies).

explanation.what_it_is: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, comprising about 30% of total protein mass. It forms the structural scaffold of skin, tendons, ligaments, bones, and connective tissue. Dietary collagen (from food or supplements) is broken down into amino acids and smaller peptides during digestion, which your body then uses to synthesize new collagen and repair tissues.
explanation.how_it_works: When you consume collagen, your digestive system breaks it into amino acids and collagen peptides. These building blocks are absorbed and transported throughout the body, where they can be incorporated into structural proteins, especially in high-turnover tissues like tendons and skin. Collagen also contains glycine and proline—amino acids that signal your fibroblasts (collagen-producing cells) to increase synthesis. Additionally, collagen peptides may modulate inflammatory pathways and support the gut barrier, which can indirectly reduce systemic inflammation and stress-related immune activation.

proven_benefits.note: Human evidence from 34 studies shows collagen supplementation reliably supports muscle strength and power output, particularly when combined with resistance training.
32 human trials demonstrate collagen accelerates recovery and strengthens damaged tendons and connective tissues, though effects are most pronounced with consistent use over weeks.
33 human studies indicate collagen modulates inflammatory markers and reduces systemic inflammation, likely through both structural repair and immune signaling.
25 human trials suggest collagen (particularly via gut-barrier support and potential effects on neurotransmitter pathways) may reduce perceived stress and anxiety symptoms.

explanation.emerging_research: Recent studies are exploring collagen's role in brain health and mood resilience, as well as its potential to support skin hydration and elasticity from within—though these areas remain early and require larger, longer trials. Some research hints that specific collagen types (e.g., Type II for joint cartilage) may have distinct benefits, but head-to-head comparisons in humans are still limited.
explanation.caveats: Collagen quality and bioavailability vary widely among supplements; hydrolyzed or peptide forms are better absorbed than intact collagen. Most benefits require consistent use over 8–12 weeks; effects are modest and work best alongside adequate vitamin C, exercise, and overall nutrition, not as a standalone remedy.
